spans.s:
bhāva
(‘emotion’)
------------------------------------------
The words ‘bhāva’ and ‘rasa’ are often used in works dealing with dramatics and poetics. A भाव is defined as a permanent or lasting emotion lying deep in the subconscious strata of our minds. When it is aesthetically excited, it produces, in a sympathetic heart, the corresponding sentiment called ‘rasa.’ Bhāvas have been listed as nine with the corresponding rasas, also nine, known as ‘navarasas’. They are:
BHĀVA RASA
1. रति (lust) śṛṅgāra (erotic)
2. hāsa (mirth) hāsya (comic)
3. śoka (sorrow) karuṇā (pathetic)
4. krodha (anger) raudra (furious)
5. utsāha (courage) vīra (heroic)
6. bhaya (fear) bhayānaka (terrible)
7. jugupsā (aversion) bībhatsa(disgusting)
8. vismaya (wonder) adbhuta(marvellous)
9. nirveda or शम (detachment, repose) śānta (peaceful)

These bhāvas considered as permanent, are sometimes called ‘sthāyī-bhāvas’ as against the transitory ones, called ‘sañcārī or vyabhicārī bhāvas.’ The latter may be as many as 33 or 34.
Eight more bhāvas or states, involuntary evidences of internal feelings like trembling, shedding tears and so on, are also mentioned sometimes, taking the total number to 50 or 51. (See also ALAṄKĀRA-ŚĀSTRA and RASAS.)
The word ‘bhāva’ in Hindu अस्त्रोलोग्य् indicates the significance of a होउसे in a होरोस्चोपे. For instance, the ‘bhāva’ of the second होउसे is dhana or wealth, and of the fifth होउसे it is पुत्र or son. So, if the प्लनेत्स् are propitiously situated with reference to the second or the fifth होउसे, he would be wealthy or have sons.

Bhavadeva-bhaṭṭa
------------------------------------------
Hindu scriptures have been classified into two groups: śruti and स्मृति. The वेदस् are the śruti, the revealed works. All other works—the works of the sages like मनु, याज्ञवल्क्य and Parāśara—which deal with more mundane matters such as आचार (personal conduct) and vyavahāra (social conduct) come under the second group. These works are also called ‘dharma-śāstras.’
The dharmaśāstra literature has grown abundantly over the centuries, due to the contributions of numerous sages, scholars and religio-social leaders. Consi-dering the needs of the contemporary society these savants added or deleted or substituted or modified the several rules given in the earlier books.
One such author was भवदेव-भट्ट, who also had the honorific ‘Bālavalabhī-bhujaṅga.’ He was the son of गोवर्धन and Sāṅgokā and belonged to the Sāvarṇa गोत्र or lineage of the Kauthumī school of Sāmaveda. The family belonged to the Siddhalagrāma in Rāhā (in Bengal). Baladevabhaṭṭa was a minister of the king Harivarmadeva. He must have lived around A.

.
The works attributed to him are: Vyavahāratilaka, Sambandhaviveka, Karmānuṣṭhānapaddhati, प्रायश्चित्त-prakaraṇa and Tautātitamatatilaka.
The first work, on judicial procedure, though quoted by some others, has not been traced till now. The second is a small work based on a part of Manusmṛti (3.5) dealing with the prohibition of endogamous marriages. The principal subjects dealt with in the third are: navagraha-होम (oblations into the duly consecrated fire to appease the nine प्लनेत्स्), mātṛpūjā (worshipping the मोथेर्), पाणिग्रहण (clasping the hand) and other rites connected with मर्रिअगे as also the other सṁस्कारस् or sacraments like उपनयन (initiation into Vedic studies). The fourth deals with the expiations for five grave sins like ब्रह्महत्या (killing a ब्राह्मण), सुरापान (drinking liquor) and so on. The last work deals with the first three adhyāyas or chapters of the Pūrvamīmāṁsā-sūtras of जैमिनि following in the footsteps of Kumārilabhaṭṭa (8th century A.D.) who was also known as Tautātita.
Bhavadevabhaṭṭa was also an expert in आयुर्वेद (life-science or medicine and surgery) and astravidyā (military scien-ces). He is supposed to have composed works on होरा or अस्त्रोलोग्य् also.

bhavapratyaya
(‘that which causes transmigration’)
------------------------------------------
The Yogasūtras of पतञ्जलि (200 B.C.) describes eight graded steps for controlling the मिन्द्. The last step is ‘samādhi,’ perfect concentration, resulting in a superconscious experience. This समाधि, again, is twofold: सम्प्रज्ञात and असम्प्रज्ञात. In the former, the object of concentration is fully revealed and known. In the latter the मिन्द् settles down into itself without any vṛttis or modifications. Hence there will be no ज्ञान or knowledge of any object in particular.
This latter समाधि is also twofold: upāyapratyaya and भवप्रत्यय. ‘Prat-yaya’ means कारण or cause. ‘Bhava’ means सṁसार or transmigratory existence. Since this latter समाधि does not give मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन्, but causes bhava or transmigration, has been rightly called ‘bhava-pratyaya.’
Some yogis, endowed with apara-वैराग्य or inferior spirit of renunciation, choose such objects as the pañca-bhūtas (the five elements such as earth and water), the इन्द्रियस् (the sense-organs) or अहङ्कार (the ego) and so on for their objects of meditation. When they attain asam-prajñāta समाधि through these, they attain a state which is similar to कैवल्य or लिबेरतिओन्. However, since they lack विवेक-ख्याति or the direct experience that the आत्मन् (the Self) is separate from प्रकृति (nature), they return to transmigratory existence after some time.
See also ASAMPRAJÑATA-SAMĀDHI, SAMĀDHI, SAMPRAJÑĀTA-SAMĀDHI and UPĀYA-PRATYAYA.

Bhāvanopaniṣad
------------------------------------------
This is a minor upaniṣad belonging to the शाक्त school, dealing with शक्ति or the Divine मोथेर् and has been classed under the Atharvaṇaveda. The शाक्त school holds that ब्रह्मन् the Absolute, the ultimate cause and substratum of this universe, is also the शक्ति or the primordial power. It is also called ‘prakāśa’ or the Supreme Light. When it deliberates to manifest the च्रेअतिओन् out of itself—the deliberation itself being called ‘vimarśa’—it results in a movement or vibration known as ‘spanda.’ The interplay of prakāśa and विमर्श increases the स्पन्द gradually, resulting in a graded manifestation of this world of name and form. The rays emerging from the supreme light in the course of various stages of manifestation array themselves in a form pattern which is now well-known as श्रीचक्र. It is a masterplan of the universe, a symbol image and abode of शक्ति or the Divine मोथेर् variously called as ललिता (the मोथेर् of grace), Rāja-rājeśvarī (Her most Imperial Majesty) or कामेश्वरी (the मोथेर् of love).
The पुराणस् describe the श्रीचक्र as the central place of the city of the great Goddess. However, this श्रीचक्र is not outside, in the external universe, but is within oneself. This upaniṣad teaches us the ‘bhāvanā’ or the right attitude or mode of meditation to rediscover the श्रीचक्र within oneself. Hence it is called Bhāvanopaniṣad.
Since whatever is in the macrocosm, is also in the microcosm, by knowing the latter one can know the former. The भावना or meditation taught here, starts from the outermost चक्र or diagram of the श्रीचक्र and traverses step by step, the whole gamut of the nine चक्रस् up to the innermost. In the aspirant, the identity is established part by part, limb by limb, from the outermost to the innermost being, the very सोउल्. As a culmination everything is experienced as pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् and one’s own body becomes full of bliss. The aspirant thus realizes the light or becomes one with it.
The Upaniṣad declares that the act of meditation is itself worship; and gives symbolic meaning of terms like अर्घ्य (water offered for washing hands) or होम (duly consecrated fire-offerings).

bhāvarūpa
(‘of the form of existence,’ ‘positive’)
------------------------------------------
According to the Advaita Vedānta philosophy our real nature is the आत्मन् or the Self which is pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्. Our इग्नोरन्चे of our real nature—technically called ‘avidyā’ or ‘ajñāna’—has led to our wrong identification with the body-मिन्द् complex resulting in सṁसार or transmigratory existence. Hence, to attain मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन्, we have to get rid of this अविद्या or अज्ञान through विद्या or ज्ञान (knowledge).
In this connection, philosophers of the Advaita school have widely discussed the nature of this अविद्या or अज्ञान and have come to the conclusion that it is ‘bhāvarūpa’ or positive and not ‘abhāva-rūpa’ or negative since it is felt or experienced. For instance, when we say, ‘I do not know anything,’ ‘I am an ignorant person’ we actually feel or experience that इग्नोरन्चे. However, its reality has not been given the status of ‘sat’ (‘that which exists’) since it can be destroyed by knowledge.
See also AJÑĀNA.

Bhavabhūti
------------------------------------------
In the classical Sanskrit literature, one of the playwrights who is often compared favourably with Kālidāsa—considered to be the greatest—is Bhava-bhūti. His original name was श्रीकण्ठ. ‘Bhavabhūti’ or ‘Bhaṭṭabhavabhūti’ was the name by which he came to be known in the annals of Sanskrit literature. His parents were Jatukarṇi and नीलकण्ठ. Jñānanidhi was his teacher. He belonged to the Kāśyapa गोत्र or lineage. He must have lived in the early part of the 8th century A.D., in Padmapura of Vidarbha-deśa (near the modern Nagpur).
Mālatīmādhava, Mahāvīracarita and Uttararāmacarita are the three well-known nāṭakas or plays authored by him. The first is a love-story whereas the latter two are stories based on the Rāmāyaṇa. The author has taken quite a bit of freedom in altering the original story to suit his purpose. His style is rather tough though elegant. Books on dramaturgy and poetics often quote from his works as ideal examples for the particular points made out by them.

Bhavatāriṇī
(‘One who causes the [jīva] to cross [the ocean of] सṁसार’)
------------------------------------------
Worship of God as the शक्ति (the Divine Power or मोथेर्) is quite ancient in the Hindu religious tradition. One of the more well-known aspects of this शक्ति, especially the fierce ones, is Kālī. Bhava-tārīṇī, which literally means ‘one who helps the जीव or the individual सोउल् to cross over सṁसार or transmigratory existence,’ is one of the names by which Kālī is known in the Bengali tradition of शक्ति worship. The deity at the famous temple of Kālī in Dakṣiṇeśvar (Calcutta) has been well-known as Bhavatāriṇi.
See KĀLĪ for details.

Bhaviṣya-purāṇa
(‘purāṇa of the future’)
------------------------------------------
Purāṇas are the mythological lore of हिन्दुइस्म् and rank among its secondary scriptures. Hindu tradition lists 18 major पुराणस् and another 18 minor पुराणस्, all ascribed to the well-known sage Veda-व्यास.
The Bhaviṣya-purāṇa has been classed among the major पुराणस् and hence sometimes called the Bhaviṣya-mahāpurāṇa also. According to one printed version, it is divided into four books: Brahmaparva, Madhyamaparva, Pratisargaparva and Uttaraparva. In all, there are 585 chapters and 26,000 ślokas. The last book is sometimes treated as an independent purāṇa entitled Bhaviṣyottara-purāṇa. Minus this book, the number of verses comes to 14,000 or 14,500, a number generally and widely accepted by the scholars based on the information given in other पुराणस् like the Matsya and the Agni.
This purāṇa belongs to the period A.

-1000. Its last book, with its many references to kings including the Muslim invaders, known to history, has been considered as having many interpolations. The first book Brāhmaparva is undoubtedly the oldest part.
As per another version, the purāṇa consists of five books: Brāhmaparva, Vaiṣṇavaparva, Śaivaparva, Sauraparva and Pratisargaparva. The total number of chapters is 605, the number of verses being 14,000.
The whole purāṇa is a miscellany dealing with a bewildering variety of subjects. The upāsanā (worship) of सूर्य, the Sun-god, has been given a prominent place. Details concerning the construction of temples, making and consecration of images, varieties of vratas or religious observances motivated by desires, sins and their expiations, दान or giving gifts—these ar some of the other subjects dealt with in the work.
The prefix ‘bhaviṣya’ (‘future’) seems to have been given to it on the assumption that though an ancient work composed by the hoary sage वेदव्यास, it predicts many events of the future.
See also PURĀṆAS.

bhāvanā
(‘that which is produced’)
------------------------------------------
Though the word is commonly used in the sense of an idea or a thought, it is frequently employed in a technical sense by several sciences.
In the न्याय-Vaiśeṣika school, it is defined as a special quality of the मिन्द्, a saṁskāra or past impression, born out of experience and giving rise to memory.
In the पूर्वमीमाṁसा school it denotes the mental activity of the person who intends to get some work done or do it himself. For instance, when Yajñadatta asks Devadatta, ‘Bring the cow,’ the mental activity of Yajñadatta that induces Devadatta to bring the cow is called ‘bhāvanā’ and is expressed through the words uttered by him. Hence it is called ‘śābdī-भावना’ or भावना related to ‘śabda’ or word. The mental activity that arises in devadatta on hearing those words is also a ‘bhāvanā;’ but it is called ‘ārthībhāvanā’ since this भावना or mental activity is related to ‘artha’ or utility.
Since the वेदस् (the कर्मकाण्ड part that prescribes rituals) are ‘apauruṣeya’ or impersonal, the शाब्दीभावना is inherent in their words of command.
The पुराणस् use the word in the sense of a deep-rooted mental impression based on which one sees the world or works in it. For instance sages like सनक or Sanandana who were endowed with ब्रह्मज्ञान or knowledge of ब्रह्मन् saw the world with ‘brahma-भावना,’ or that it is ब्रह्मन् itself. Ordinary gods and human beings endowed with ‘karma-भावना’ saw it as fit for action. Extraordi-nary deities like the हिरण्यगर्भ who had ‘brahma-कर्म-भावना,’ saw it as ब्रह्मन् but also fit for discharging the duties (karma = action, duties) allotted to them.
In आयुर्वेद the word ‘bhāvanā’ stands for the process of dissolving some powders of medical qualities in appropriate solvents to prepare the medicine.

Bhavānī
(‘consort of Bhava or शिव’)
------------------------------------------
Śiva, the last of the Hindu Trinity, is called ‘Bhava’ since the च्रेअतिओन् comes into being (bhavati asmāt) out of Him. पार्वती, His consort is therefore known as ‘Bhavānī.’
See PĀRVATĪ.
